title: Fluid Mechanics
summary: Fluids exert pressure that increases with depth ($P=P_0+\rho gh$). Buoyancy (Archimedes) lifts submerged objects by the weight of displaced fluid. Flowing fluids obey continuity ($Av$ constant) and Bernoulli's equation relating pressure, speed, and height.

pressure.plain: Force per unit area in a fluid.
pressure.in_class: $P=F/A$, in pascals; acts in all directions.

pressure with depth.plain: Pressure rises with depth in a fluid.

buoyant force.plain: Upward force on a submerged object.
buoyant force.in_class: Equals the weight of displaced fluid (Archimedes).

continuity equation.plain: Flow rate is constant along a pipe.

Pascal's principle.plain: Pressure applied to a fluid transmits undiminished.

concept_sections.heading: Pressure and depth
concept_sections.explanation: Pressure in a static fluid increases with depth: $P=P_0+\rho gh$. It acts equally in all directions at a point.
math_steps: Pressure is the same at equal depths.

concept_sections.heading: Buoyancy
concept_sections.explanation: A submerged object feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces: $F_b=\rho_{fluid}Vg$. It floats if $F_b\ge$ weight.

concept_sections.heading: Pascal's principle and hydraulics
concept_sections.explanation: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmits equally everywhere, so a small force on a small piston lifts a large load on a big piston: $F_1/A_1=F_2/A_2$.

concept_sections.heading: Continuity
concept_sections.explanation: For incompressible flow, what enters must exit: $A_1v_1=A_2v_2$. A narrower pipe means faster flow.

concept_sections.heading: Bernoulli's equation
concept_sections.explanation: Along a streamline, $P+\tfrac12\rho v^2+\rho gh$ is constant — faster flow means lower pressure. It explains lift and flow through pipes.

real_world_examples.title: Why ships float
real_world_examples.scenario: A steel ship floats though steel sinks.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Its shape displaces enough water that buoyancy equals the ship's weight.

real_world_examples.title: A hydraulic car lift
real_world_examples.scenario: A small pump raises a heavy car.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Pascal's principle multiplies force by the piston-area ratio.

real_world_examples.title: Airplane lift / a shower curtain
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Bernoulli's equation links higher speed to lower pressure, creating lift or suction.

problems.prompt: Find the pressure $10$ m deep in water ($\rho=1000$, ignore atmosphere).
Find the density of a $6$ kg object of volume $0.002$ m³.
An object displaces $0.01$ m³ of water. Find the buoyant force.
Water flows at $2$ m/s in a pipe of area $0.1$ m². Find the speed where the area is $0.05$ m².
A hydraulic lift: $F_1=100$ N on $A_1=0.01$ m². Find the lift force on $A_2=0.5$ m².
Find the total pressure $5$ m deep in water (add atmosphere $1.0\times10^5$ Pa).
A block of density $600$ kg/m³ floats in water. What fraction is submerged?
problems.hint: Float fraction is the density ratio.
